A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FM-DD/FM-RE research. Their main text, equations, proofs, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including content moved between the appendices and main text.

before.justification: Sections 6.1–6.3 and Appendix D report original synthetic-generation, constrained MNIST-generation, and adversarial-image experiments, with distributional metrics, constraint violations, and classification results.

after.justification: Section 6 and Appendix C report original generation and adversarial-image results, alongside additional baseline comparisons, training-time measurements, and gradient diagnostics.

M1.justification: Appendix C.1.2 introduces and tests an FM-RE gradient-estimation variant that subtracts a constant baseline b=1 from the terminal constraint indicator. The core FM-DD objective, two-stage FM-RE procedure, and sampling algorithms remain unchanged; the adversarial-generation adaptation was already documented in v1.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same five synthetic cases, MNIST brightness and thickness constraints, and adversarial generation for MNIST/LeNet-5 and CIFAR-10/ResNet-50. The new fine-tuning and gradient analyses operate within existing synthetic tasks.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated NAMM and PDM baselines across the synthetic cases in Table 2, PDM for MNIST brightness in Table 3, and a fine-tuned FM comparator in Appendix C.1.1. NAMM and PDM were cited in v1 but did not participate in these comparisons. This substantially broadens the empirical comparison set.

E3.justification: v2 adds a controlled with/without-baseline evaluation using fixed model parameters at each epoch and gradient-norm/variance measurements, plus absolute training-time comparisons across methods. Existing data splits, generation sample counts, SWD/FID evaluations, and tabulated FM-DD/FM-RE hyperparameters are retained.

E4.justification: New Appendix C.1.1 compares joint optimization with fine-tuning and examines distribution distortion. Appendix C.1.2 adds an ablation testing whether baseline subtraction reduces gradient noise, while Table 4 quantifies comparative training costs. These substantially extend analysis beyond the retained parameter sweeps and adversarial noise controls.

E5.justification: Figure 6 introduces gradient statistics computed from 100 repetitions of an epoch with model parameters fixed. This adds a statistical estimation procedure; the existing 100-generation-trial averaging and synthetic mean-plus-standard-deviation reporting remain unchanged. The PDFs do not report an increase in independent training runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds NAMM/PDM scores, fine-tuning results, runtime measurements, and gradient curves. MDM's Box SWD changes from 0.2764 ± 0.0874 to 0.1431 ± 0.0747. Between v1 Table 8 and v2 Table 9, Gaussian-noise norms change from 5.59 to 5.47 for MNIST and 10.94 to 11.15 for CIFAR-10; CIFAR-10 accuracy changes from 84.1% to 82.3%. Original headline FM-DD/FM-RE scores remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix B adds a derivation showing that a state-dependent baseline has zero expected score-function contribution and gives the corresponding unbiased gradient expression in Equations 22–23. The original propositions and proofs are otherwise substantially retained, with clarified trajectory notation.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain differentiable-distance penalization, oracle-based randomized exploration, computationally efficient two-stage training, and constrained/adversarial generation applications. The abstract explicitly identifies the existing one-stage efficiency comparison, and the conclusion emphasizes both methods without materially redefining the contributions.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretation through explanations of PDM/NAMM distribution mismatch, joint optimization versus fine-tuning and forgetting, baseline-induced variance reduction, and constraint-dependent computational overhead. The principal limitations already existed in v1 Appendix C and are relocated. The explicit statement that thickness FID worsens is removed, although Table 3 retains the adverse values.

D1.justification: v2 adds per-experiment training times, practical starting recommendations for lambda, t0, and N2, and clearer descriptions of comparator requirements and subspace information access. These extend documentation; the reported GPU, experiment-specific parameter table, and code-access link are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds Uehara et al. (2024) and explicitly distinguishes joint optimization from reinforcement-learning-based fine-tuning. It expands discussion of the already-cited PDM and clarifies NAMM's differentiable-distance requirement. The broader positioning against reflection and mirror-map approaches remains intact.

P1.justification: v2 removes 'Efficient' from the title, edits the abstract and explanatory passages, expands the conclusion, and adds hyperparameter guidance. It moves the adversarial formulation and limitations into the main text and renames the experimental appendix from D to C. Most section ordering and existing prose remain recognizable.

P2.justification: v2 adds fine-tuning and gradient-diagnostic figures and a training-time table, expands comparison tables, and visually groups existing adversarial examples. The TMLR format changes front matter, headers, typography, and display placement, including placing Figure 2 beside Table 3. The combined display and layout revision is substantial.

improvement.justification: The NAMM/PDM evaluations address an important gap in v1's comparisons with methods applicable beyond simple convex constraints. The gradient-baseline proof and ablation, fine-tuning comparison, and runtime table substantially strengthen assessment of optimization behavior and practical trade-offs. Although v2 softens discussion of the unchanged thickness-FID disadvantage, its numerical evidence and principal limitations remain disclosed, yielding a clear net improvement.
